string.text: Many people across the Americas trace their ancestry to Akan-speaking populations due to the trans-Atlantic slave trade. Between the 17th and 19th centuries, a significant proportion of enslaved Africans shipped from the Gold Coast — estimated at 10% of all embarkations from West Africa — were of Akan origin. Although gold remained central to the Akan economy, the intensification of internal conflicts — especially among the Fante and Ashanti during the 18th century — led to the capture and external sale of war captives, many of whom were exported through coastal ports such as Anomabo and Cape Coast.
Maroon Warlords
Za of Maroon

The Maroons hold the southeastern extremity of the Aserai lands, where the Jabal al-Kals - the hills of bitterness - run down to the shore of the Bahr al-Yeshm and divide the sultanate from the Empire. In 1080 a large number of Akan freedom fighters already living in those hills launched an assault on the Northern Empire in Calradia, freeing between 300 and 400 enslaved people. They established a new community of free people in the broken country above the coastal road, where imperial cavalry could not follow them. Naquan, Cudjoe's father, was allegedly the one who orchestrated this rebellion. Naquan was succeeded by Cudjoe, the first Za of this group of Maroons.
Maroon Warlords
I am {CONVERSATION_CHARACTER.LINK} of the {CLAN_NAME}, my {?PLAYER.GENDER}lady{?}lord{\?}, and I am honored to serve you.
I am {CONVERSATION_CHARACTER.LINK} of the {CLAN_NAME}. My oath to your banner is my bond — I do not give it lightly, my {?PLAYER.GENDER}lady{?}lord{\?}.
I am {CONVERSATION_CHARACTER.LINK} of the {CLAN_NAME}. You will find no fiercer sword arm in your service, my {?PLAYER.GENDER}lady{?}lord{\?}.
I am {CONVERSATION_CHARACTER.LINK} of the {CLAN_NAME}. Alliance with you is sound strategy. I trust it will prove so for us both, my {?PLAYER.GENDER}lady{?}lord{\?}.
I am {CONVERSATION_CHARACTER.LINK} of the {CLAN_NAME}.
I am {CONVERSATION_CHARACTER.LINK} of the {CLAN_NAME}. My word is my only currency — spend it wisely.
I am {CONVERSATION_CHARACTER.LINK} of the {CLAN_NAME}. I have bled for these lands. Do not make me regret that.
I am {CONVERSATION_CHARACTER.LINK} of the {CLAN_NAME}. Come in peace and you will find it returned.
I am {CONVERSATION_CHARACTER.LINK} of the {CLAN_NAME}. Let us be direct — what do you want, and what will it cost me?
I am {CONVERSATION_CHARACTER.LINK} of the {CLAN_NAME}. I have little time and less patience. Speak your purpose.
I am {CONVERSATION_CHARACTER.LINK}, of {CLAN_NAME}.
I am {CONVERSATION_CHARACTER.LINK}, of {CLAN_NAME}. We have kept our honour when others cast theirs aside.
I am {CONVERSATION_CHARACTER.LINK}, of {CLAN_NAME}. We do not forget those who showed us kindness.
I am {CONVERSATION_CHARACTER.LINK}, of {CLAN_NAME}. You would do well to remember both names.
I am {CONVERSATION_CHARACTER.LINK}, of {CLAN_NAME}. Those who crossed us have learned what that means.
I am {CONVERSATION_CHARACTER.LINK}, Za of the {CLAN_NAME}. My father's father fought for these mountains. I will not surrender a stone of them.
I am {CONVERSATION_CHARACTER.LINK}, Za of the {CLAN_NAME}. Sankofa — we look back so we do not lose our way forward.
I am {CONVERSATION_CHARACTER.LINK} of the {CLAN_NAME}. You stand in the presence of a Maroon matriarch — mind your manners.
I am {CONVERSATION_CHARACTER.LINK} of the {CLAN_NAME}. My hearth is open to those who come in friendship.
I am {CONVERSATION_CHARACTER.LINK} of the {CLAN_NAME}. My people have survived worse than you — I ask only that you give me reason to trust.
rightful Za of the Maroon
rightful Za of the Maroon
You fought well. We did not seek this quarrel, but you left us no choice. Rest — we are not savages.
Did you truly believe you could ride into Maroon lands and leave unscathed? You will have time in that cell to reconsider.
A warrior deserves a warrior's treatment. You have that, at least, from me.
You are unharmed — I have given orders. I hope you will remember that when the time comes to speak of us to others.
The mountains demanded a price. We paid it. Now let us see to our wounded.
We fought as our ancestors taught — without fear, without hesitation. This victory belongs to every soul that bled for Maroon freedom.
We chose our ground, we chose our moment. This was never in doubt.
Let word of this spread. The next column that marches into these hills will think twice.
A decisive victory. The Adinkra say 'Aya' — the fern endures. So must we.
Well fought. Honour demands I say so plainly — you have earned respect this day.
The outcome was the correct one. I trust our arrangement remains intact.
The Maroons have never sought war for its own sake. We fight because we must. If there is a path through words, I would walk it.
Enough lives have been spent. Let us speak of what a lasting peace might look like for both our peoples.
Continuing this costs us both. I am prepared to discuss terms — if you are prepared to be reasonable.
You are riding on Maroon land. State your business, and state it plainly.
I have not run from a fight in forty years. I will not start now. Choose your next words carefully.
I know what you are doing. I know why. And I know exactly how this ends if you do not stand down.
The last man who challenged me this way is no longer a concern. Yours is a short road.
Word of your deeds travels faster than you do. Do not expect a warm welcome in these mountains.
We built our freedom on the principle that no one owns another. What you have done is an affront to everything the Maroons stand for.
I am cataloguing what you have done. Debts are not forgotten here.
There are few in Calradia I would call worthy of respect. You are closer to that list than most.
What you did was right. Simple as that. I will not pretend otherwise.
Kindness is rarely repaid in kind in this world. The Maroons remember those who break that pattern.
Akwaaba — you are welcome among us. Sit, eat, tell me what the roads are saying.
Good to see you riding these roads again. My cook has prepared more than we can eat — come, join us.
The Maroons do not take oaths lightly, and we do not release them lightly. Think carefully before you bind yourself to us — or before you leave.
You are leaving. I will not grovel. But know that a soldier's worth is measured in loyalty as much as in skill.
Gao Castle

Faso lies on the desert-steppe east of the Bahr al-Yeshm, in the long shadow of the Jabal al-Kals. Villagers sink wells deep into the gravel and trap what little runoff comes down from the bitter hills, using it to water their groves of date palms.
Cudjoes Town

Cudjoes Town sits high on the seaward slopes of the Jabal al-Kals, the bitter hills, where the Aserai deserts give way to scrub and acacia. The villagers terrace the hillsides for olives, and keep watch over the coastal road below - the highway that caravans and armies have used between the Empire and the Aserai lands for thousands of years.
Abrafo Castle

Assin lies in the shallow bowl below Abrafo Castle, close enough that the castle horn carries to the fields. Its people owe the garrison dates rather than silver, an arrangement they negotiated themselves and defend whenever a steward proposes otherwise.

Denkyira takes its name from a kingdom that ruled the Akan goldfields and then lost them. The villagers are said to descend from that court, and they keep the name deliberately, as a caution about what becomes of those who hold others in bondage.
Nanny Town

Nanny Town is built on a shelf of rock reachable by one path, which its founders chose so that it could be held by a handful of people against a column. Whether the woman it is named for ever lived there is disputed even among the Maroons, but the town has never been taken, and its people regard that as the more useful fact.

Accompong is the granary of Nanny Town, laid out on the only ground on this side of the range flat enough to take a plough. Its headmen sit in the town assembly by right rather than by invitation, a concession won during the first siege and never given back.
Scotts Hall

Scotts Hall keeps the name of the estate that once stood here and of the man who ran it, which visitors often find strange. The villagers say they kept it so that nobody would have to be told what the terraces were built for, or by whom.
Trelawny Keep
Moore Town

Moore Town lies west of Trelawny Keep where the range begins to break into gullies. It is the last Maroon settlement before Khuzait country, and its herds are kept close to the houses at night for reasons the villagers consider too obvious to explain.
Charles Town

Charles Town is the newest of the Maroon villages, settled by people who came over the hills long after the first rising and were given land on the exposed southern face because it was what remained. They have made more of it than anyone expected.
Kormantse Castle

Anomabo is named for a port on the far Gold Coast that most of its people have never seen and their grandparents were carried away from. The flocks are folded against the castle wall each night, a habit from the years when the Maroons owned nothing they could not drive uphill at short notice.

Adanse holds the open ground north of Kormantse Castle, where the hills flatten enough to run horses. The stock is descended from animals taken in the rising, and the villagers will tell you at length that no Maroon has ever bought a horse from anyone who once owned people.
